barcode-scanner: Reads a price at the checkout in a blink. A laser spot sweeps across printed stripes, and a photocell turns the flicker of reflected light, strong from the white gaps and weak from the black bars, into a number the computer looks up.
catalytic-converter: The box in a car's exhaust that removes most of its poisons. Hot exhaust passes over a ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum, which speeds up the reactions that turn carbon monoxide, unburned fuel and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen, without being used up itself.
ccd: The chip that replaced film in cameras and telescopes. Light falling on each pixel knocks electrons loose, so the brighter the spot the more charge collects; the charges are then shuffled out row by row and counted.
cochlear-implant: Gives hearing to people who are profoundly deaf. A microphone and chip split sound into pitches, and a row of electrodes threaded into the inner ear gives tiny shocks to the hearing nerve at the right places, which the brain learns to hear as sound.
computer-mouse: A pointer you move by hand. A rubber ball underneath grips the desk and rolls rather than slides, turning two small wheels at right angles, so the computer can count how far the hand moved left-right and up-down.
dna-sequencing: Reads the letters of a gene, and later of the whole human genome. Copies of the DNA are made that stop at each letter, and the pieces are pulled through a gel, where shorter ones travel faster, so their order spells out the sequence.
dram: The working memory of every computer. Each bit is a small electric charge parked on a microscopic capacitor next to a transistor switch. The charge leaks away, so the chip tops it up thousands of times a second.
hard-disk-drive: A computer's long-term memory. A head floating a hair's width above a spinning platter flips the direction of tiny magnetized patches, one bit each, and they keep their direction with the power off.
hovercraft: A craft that travels over water, mud, sand or ice alike. A fan blows air under the hull, where a rubber skirt holds it in; the trapped air is squeezed and pushes back hard enough to lift the craft off the surface, so there is almost no friction.
induction-cooktop: A stove top that heats the pan but not itself. A coil under the glass makes a rapidly changing magnetic field, which stirs up swirling currents inside the iron pan, and the pan's own resistance turns them into heat.
inkjet-printer: The everyday home printer. Behind each of hundreds of tiny nozzles a crystal flexes when given a voltage and squirts out a droplet of ink, thousands of times a second, while motors step the head across the page and feed the paper.
kevlar: The fibre in bulletproof vests, five times stronger than steel for its weight. Its molecules are stiff rods that line up by themselves in a liquid-crystal solution, and spinning the solution into a fibre freezes them in line, so a pull is taken by the strong bonds along every molecule.
laser-rangefinder: Measures distance by timing light, from surveyors' tools to the distance to the Moon. A laser fires a short pulse, a photocell catches its reflection, and since light's speed is known exactly, the round-trip time gives the distance, to within centimetres even off mirrors left on the Moon.
lcd: The flat screen of watches, laptops and TVs. A film of liquid crystal sits between two crossed polarizing sheets; its molecules twist the light so it gets through, and a small voltage straightens them so that dot goes dark.
microwave-oven: Heats food in a minute or two. A magnetron fills the box with microwaves, which water molecules soak up by jiggling back and forth billions of times a second, so the food heats from the inside while the plate stays cool.
mri: Takes detailed pictures of soft tissue like the brain, with no radiation. In a very strong magnet the hydrogen nuclei in the body's water all line up; a radio pulse tips them over, they ring back with faint radio signals, and a computer works out where each signal came from.
reverse-osmosis: How most of the world's desalination plants make drinking water from the sea. A thin plastic membrane lets water molecules through but not salt; normally water would flow toward the salty side, but pushing the sea water hard enough forces it the other way.
smoke-detector: The cheap ceiling alarm found in most homes. A speck of radioactive americium knocks electrons off air molecules, so a small current flows across a gap; smoke particles soak up the charged molecules, the current drops, and the alarm sounds.
superconducting-magnet: The powerful magnets inside MRI scanners and particle accelerators. Coils of special wire, cooled by liquid helium to a few degrees above absolute zero, lose all electrical resistance, so they carry enormous currents with no heat and no power once started.
thermal-camera: Sees people, animals and hot engines in total darkness or smoke, used by firefighters and soldiers. Everything warm gives off infrared light, the warmer the brighter; a special lens and sensor chip turn that invisible glow into a picture.
touchscreen: A screen you point at with a finger, as on every phone. A grid of transparent electrodes under the glass holds a small charge; a fingertip, which conducts, draws some of it away, and the chip finds the spot where the charge dropped.
ultrasound-scanner: Lets doctors see inside the body without X-rays, most famously the unborn child. A probe sends pulses of very high-pitched sound and listens for the faint echoes from every boundary between organs; the timing of each echo places it on a screen.
video-tape-recorder: A tape recorder fast enough for television. A spinning electromagnet head lines up the tiny atomic magnets in a coated plastic tape, so the picture is kept as a trail of magnetized spots that can be played back the same evening.
ft-limestone-heat-battery: Future Technology 1. Solar power stops at night, and batteries big enough to cover it are costly. By day, concentrated sunlight bakes limestone, driving off carbon dioxide, and the lime and the gas are kept in separate tanks, which can hold the energy for months. At night the gas is let back onto the lime, which soaks it up and gets very hot, raising steam to spin a turbine; limestone is cheap and found almost everywhere.
ft-moire-swelling-band: Future Technology 2. About one in five breast-cancer survivors gets lymphedema, a lifelong arm swelling that is easiest to reverse in its first millimetres, yet it is checked with a tape measure at clinic visits. A stretchy band carries two overlapping fine-line prints; when the arm grows even a millimetre around, the lines shift and broad stripes slide visibly along the band (moiré), so the wearer sees the change every morning.
ft-nanotube-skyhook: Future Technology 3. Rockets spend most of their fuel just reaching orbital speed, which is why getting to space is costly. A cable of carbon nanotubes runs from a base at sea on the equator straight up, past the height where a satellite circles once a day, to a counterweight beyond it; the Earth's spin flings the counterweight outward and keeps the cable taut. Electric climbers, powered by sunlight or a laser beamed from the ground, ride up the cable carrying payloads to orbit at the cost of electricity.
ft-greenhouse-pollinating-robot: Future Technology 4. Bees are dying off, about a third of our food depends on pollinators, and indoor farms have no bees at all. Rather than a tiny flying robo-bee, which would need batteries far smaller and stronger than any we have, this is a full-size robot arm that rolls along greenhouse rows on mains power. Its camera finds open flowers and it dabs pollen from one onto another with a soft brush or puff of air, so each flower can set fruit without insects.
adiabatic-heating-and-cooling: Squeeze air quickly and it gets hot; let it expand quickly and it gets cold, even with no heat going in or out. Erasmus Darwin described air chilling as it rushed out of an air gun in 1788. Squeezing ignites fuel in diesel engines, and expanding air cools airliner cabins and makes clouds.
avalanche-breakdown: In a strong enough electric field, one free electron speeds up, smashes loose another, and those two free two more, until a flood of current pours through a gas or crystal that normally blocks it. John Townsend explained the cascade in gases around 1901. It makes Geiger counters click and lets light sensors catch single photons.
centrifugal-force: Anything going round in a circle seems flung outward, pressing harder the faster it spins: water stays in a bucket swung overhead. Christiaan Huygens worked out its size in 1659. Spin it fast enough and it squeezes water from clothes, cream from milk and heavy particles from light ones.
corona-discharge: Around a sharp point or thin wire at high voltage, the air starts to glow faintly blue and hiss as it becomes electrically charged, without a spark jumping. Sailors called it St Elmo's fire; Frank Peek worked out when it starts in 1915. It charges the drum in photocopiers, cleans soot from chimney smoke and makes ozone.
detonation: In some explosives the burning doesn't spread layer by layer like a fire; it rides a shock wave that tears through the material faster than sound, crushing as it goes. Berthelot and Vieille in Paris measured these flame fronts in gas-filled tubes in 1881. It's why dynamite shatters rock while gunpowder only pushes, and it lets welders bang dissimilar metals together into one plate.
dielectric-heating: Radio waves or microwaves make water and other polar molecules in food flip back and forth billions of times a second, and the jostling heats the food from inside. Percy Spencer at Raytheon noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket next to a radar magnetron in 1945 and built the first microwave oven. The same trick welds plastic sheets and dries timber.
eddy-currents: Move a magnet past a sheet of copper or aluminium and swirling currents spring up in the metal, dragging against the motion and warming it. Foucault showed in 1855 that a copper disc spun between magnet poles slows down and heats up. A magnet dropped down a copper pipe drifts down slowly as if through syrup, and the same drag stops trains and sorts drink cans.
electrostatic-induction: Hold a charged rod near a metal can without touching it and the can's own charges shift, so the near side becomes opposite to the rod and the can rolls toward it. John Canton in London described it in 1753. Touching the far side briefly lets you charge things over and over from one source, which is how the electrophorus and the Wimshurst machine work.
friction: Push a box across the floor and the floor pushes back. Amontons found the drag is proportional to how hard the surfaces press together, and oddly doesn't depend on how big the contact area is. Friction is what lets shoes grip, brakes stop cars and matches light.
joule-heating: Current flowing through a wire heats it, in proportion to the wire's resistance and the square of the current, so doubling the current gives four times the heat. James Joule measured it in 1841, before his famous work on the mechanical equivalent of heat.
liquid-crystals: Some substances flow like a liquid yet keep their rod-shaped molecules lined up like a crystal, so a small voltage can swing them round and change how light passes. Friedrich Reinitzer noticed in Prague in 1888 that a compound from carrots melted twice, first to a cloudy liquid, then to a clear one.
magnetic-hysteresis: Iron remembers: magnetise it and switch the field off and some magnetism stays, and to undo it you must push the other way; push hard enough and it stops responding at all (saturation). Emil Warburg measured this loop in 1880 and James Ewing, working in Japan, named it hysteresis a few years later.
moire-effect: Lay one fine grid or striped screen over another at a slight angle and broad wavy bands appear that neither pattern has, sweeping across when one layer moves a hair. Lord Rayleigh pointed out in 1874 that these bands could test how evenly a diffraction grating was ruled. Because the bands magnify tiny shifts, they are used to measure small movements and strains and to make banknotes hard to copy.
nucleation: Bubbles, droplets and crystals don't form evenly through a liquid or gas; they start on a speck, a scratch or a seed, which is why soda fizzes from the same spots on a glass. John Aitken showed around 1880 that water vapour won't form fog droplets without dust specks to start on. Supplying the right seeds makes rain, crystals or bubbles appear on command, from cloud seeding to click-to-start hand warmers.
photoconductivity: Some materials, like selenium, let electricity through far more easily in light than in the dark. Willoughby Smith noticed in 1873 that the selenium resistors he used to test undersea telegraph cables gave readings that changed with the sunlight. Light meters, dusk-to-dawn streetlight switches, early TV cameras and the drum in every photocopier and laser printer use it.
photodissociation: Light with enough energy can snap molecules apart, which is why sunlight fades dyes and turns some silver salts black. Johann Heinrich Schulze found in 1717 that silver salts darkened where light hit them, not where heat did, the effect photography later built on. High in the sky, ultraviolet light splitting oxygen molecules is what makes the ozone layer.
photophoresis: Tiny specks of dust or smoke drift along a strong light beam, or even against it, because the side the light heats pushes harder on the surrounding gas. Felix Ehrenhaft described it in 1918. Researchers use it to trap and steer single particles in mid-air, including a 2018 display that draws glowing 3D images with a laser-held speck.
piezoresistive-effect: Stretch or squeeze a wire or a chip of silicon and its electrical resistance changes, so measuring the resistance tells you the force. Lord Kelvin found it in metals in 1856, and in 1954 Charles Smith found it is many times stronger in silicon and germanium. Strain gauges in scales and bridges, car engine pressure sensors and airbag crash sensors use it.
radioluminescence: Some materials glow when struck by radiation from radioactive substances, each particle making a tiny flash of light. In 1903 William Crookes looked through a lens at a zinc sulfide screen near a speck of radium, saw it sparkle with countless separate flashes, and built the spinthariscope to show it. Tritium-lit watch hands and exit signs, and the scintillation counters that detect radiation, use it.
resonance-vibration: Push a swing in time with its own rhythm and each small push adds up until it flies high; anything that can vibrate, from a wine glass to a bridge to an electric circuit, responds hugely to pushes at its own natural frequency and hardly at all to others. Galileo described it in 1638, noting that well-timed puffs of breath could set a heavy pendulum swinging. Radios tune to one station this way, quartz watches keep time by it, and MRI scanners use it to pick out hydrogen atoms.
stroboscopic-effect: A spinning wheel lit by a flashing light seems to stand still, or creep slowly backwards, when the flashes keep pace with its turning. Plateau and Stampfer built spinning slotted discs around it in 1832, and mechanics still use it to read the speed of engines and machines without touching them.
supercooling: Very clean, still water can be cooled well below freezing and stay liquid, then turn to ice in a flash when shaken or seeded. Fahrenheit saw it in sealed bulbs of water in 1724; dropping dry ice into supercooled clouds later became cloud seeding, and supercooling now keeps donor organs alive longer without freezing them.
superheating: Water heated in a very clean, smooth container can rise above its boiling point without boiling, then erupt all at once when disturbed. Donny heated air-free water far past 100 degrees in the 1840s; Glaser later used a superheated liquid to make the bubble chamber, where passing particles leave trails of bubbles.
supersaturation: A hot liquid can dissolve extra salt or sugar and keep it dissolved as it cools, until a speck or a jolt makes it all crystallise at once. Lowitz studied these overloaded solutions and seeding them with a crystal in the 1790s; the same trick makes clickable hand warmers and, in air, the cloud trails of the cloud chamber.
total-internal-reflection: Light inside glass or water that hits the surface at a low enough angle is reflected back completely, as if the surface were a perfect mirror. Kepler described it in 1611; it keeps light trapped inside optical fibres for kilometres and folds the light path in binocular prisms.
townsend-discharge: In a gas under a strong voltage, one stray electron knocks loose others, which knock loose more, until a whole avalanche of charge rushes across. Townsend worked out this chain reaction around 1897, and it lets a Geiger counter turn the passage of one particle into a loud click.
tyndall-effect: A beam of light shining through smoke, fog or milky water becomes visible from the side because tiny particles scatter it. Tyndall studied it in 1869; it let Zsigmondy's ultramicroscope see particles too small for ordinary microscopes, and it's how many smoke alarms sense smoke.
flush-toilet: Carries waste away and keeps the smell out of the house. Pulling a handle opens a valve so water from a cistern rushes through the bowl and down the drain. Afterwards some water stays trapped in a bend of the pipe, a plug of liquid that sewer gas cannot get past.
refrigerated-transport: Lets meat, fruit and milk cross oceans without spoiling, which is why shops sell food from the other side of the world. A machine on board squeezes air, cools it with seawater, then lets it expand; air that expands gets very cold, and it is blown through an insulated hold kept below freezing.
hydroelectric-power-station: Makes electricity from falling water. A dam holds back a river, and water rushing down a pipe through the dam spins the curved blades of a turbine; the turbine's shaft turns a generator above it, where magnets sweep past coils of copper wire and push a current through them.
dishwasher: Washes a load of plates without anyone scrubbing them. Dishes stand in wire racks while a pump sprays very hot, soapy water up at them from arms below; the jets push the arms round so the spray sweeps every plate. Cochrane's first machine turned a wheel of racks through jets of hot water instead.
electric-car: A carriage that runs on stored electricity instead of horses or petrol, quiet and without exhaust. A bank of lead-acid batteries feeds an electric motor that turns the wheels; around 1900 electric cars outsold petrol ones in some cities. Today's carry lithium-ion cells under the floor, and their motors run as generators when braking.
tractor: Pulls ploughs, harvesters and trailers, doing the work of a team of horses without fields of oats to feed them. A petrol or diesel engine turns the big rear wheels through low gears that trade speed for pulling force, and deep treads dig into the soil so the wheels grip instead of spinning.
escalator: Carries a steady stream of people between floors. A motor drives a loop of chain linking a staircase of metal steps; each step rides on two pairs of wheels in separate tracks, so its tread stays level as it climbs and folds flat into a moving floor at top and bottom. A rubber handrail runs alongside at the same speed.
vacuum-cleaner: Sucks dust out of carpets instead of just stirring it into the air. A motor spins a fan that throws air out of the machine, lowering the pressure inside, so outside air rushes in through the nozzle, dragging dirt with it. A cloth bag or filter lets the air out but keeps the dust.
air-conditioning: Keeps buildings cool and dry in hot weather. A liquid refrigerant evaporates inside a coil indoors, soaking up heat from the air blown across it, while water from the air condenses on the cold fins; a compressor then squeezes the vapour so it gets hot and dumps that heat outdoors through a second coil.
geothermal-power: Makes electricity from the heat inside the Earth. Wells drilled deep into hot rock bring up steam, or water hot enough to flash into steam, and the steam spins a turbine that drives a generator. The cooled water is pumped back underground to be heated again.
water-chlorination: Makes tap water safe from cholera and typhoid. A small, measured dose of chlorine is mixed into the water at the treatment works, where it chemically burns through the outer walls and enzymes of bacteria and kills them. A faint trace stays in the pipes, so germs that get in later die too.
washing-machine: Washes a load of clothes without anyone scrubbing or wringing by hand. An electric motor turns a perforated drum, or a paddle in a tub, back and forth so soapy water is pushed through the cloth again and again; then the drum spins fast, flinging the water out through its holes.
Alva J. Fisher, Hurley Machine Company
stainless-steel: Steel that does not rust, for cutlery, sinks and surgical tools. About an eighth of it is chromium, which reacts with oxygen in the air to form a clear layer of chromium oxide only a few atoms thick. The film seals the iron off from water, and if it is scratched it forms again within moments.
zipper: Closes a jacket, bag or tent in one pull. Each metal or plastic tooth has a bump on top and a hollow underneath; the Y-shaped slider bends the two rows apart and feeds them together at an angle, so each tooth nests between two teeth on the other side and the bumps lock into the hollows.
tower-crane: Lifts steel and concrete to the top of tall buildings as they go up. A slim lattice mast carries a long horizontal arm that swings round; electric motors wind a steel cable over a trolley that runs out along the arm, and heavy concrete blocks on a short arm at the back balance the load.
traffic-light: Lets cars at a crossroads take turns instead of colliding. Coloured lamps, red for stop and green for go with amber in between, switch in a fixed cycle set by a timer or by sensors buried in the road, so each direction of traffic gets its turn.
sewage-treatment: Cleans a town's waste water before it goes back into a river. Sewage is held in tanks while air is bubbled through it, and swarms of bacteria eat the dissolved filth; the bacteria clump into a sludge that settles out, leaving clear water, and some of the sludge is fed back to start on the next batch.
drywall: Lets builders put up smooth indoor walls in a day instead of plastering for a week. Wet gypsum plaster is spread between two sheets of thick paper and sets hard as its crystals regrow. Those crystals hold water locked inside them, so in a fire the board gives off steam and slows the flames.
hybrid-corn: Gave farmers maize that grows bigger and yields far more grain. Breeders self-pollinate corn for several generations to make pure but weak inbred lines, then cross two unrelated lines. The seed from that cross grows unusually vigorous and even, but its own seed does not, so farmers buy fresh seed every year.
George Shull, Donald Jones, Henry A. Wallace
frozen-food: Keeps food tasting fresh for months. Packed food is pressed between metal plates or belts chilled far below freezing, so it freezes solid in minutes rather than hours. Fast freezing forms ice crystals too small to burst the food's cells, so it is not mushy when thawed.
prestressed-concrete: Lets concrete beams span long gaps without cracking. Steel cables running through the beam are stretched tight and anchored at the ends, squeezing the concrete hard; concrete is strong when squeezed but weak when stretched, so when a load bends the beam, its underside only loses some of that squeeze instead of being pulled apart.
fibreglass: Glass spun into strands finer than a hair. A loose wool of it traps air and insulates houses; strands set in plastic resin make light, strong boats, car bodies and wind-turbine blades. Molten glass runs through hundreds of tiny holes in a hot metal plate and is pulled out into threads so thin they bend instead of snapping.
Games Slayter and Dale Kleist, Owens-Illinois
plastics-polyethylene: The commonest plastic, used for bags, bottles, film and cable insulation. It is made by linking thousands of small molecules of ethylene gas end to end into long chains of carbon atoms; the tangled chains slide past each other when warm, so it can be moulded, but hold together as a tough, waxy solid when cool.
blood-bank: Keeps donated blood ready for operations and emergencies. The blood is mixed with sodium citrate, which stops it clotting by mopping up the calcium that clotting needs, and kept in a refrigerator just above freezing. Each bottle is marked with its blood type so it can go to a patient whose body won't attack it.
heat-pump: Heats a building with a third or less of the electricity a heater would use. It is a refrigerator run backwards: a cold refrigerant evaporates in an outdoor coil, soaking up warmth even from chilly air, ground or river water; a compressor squeezes the vapour hot, and it gives that heat up indoors as it condenses.
gas-turbine-power-station: Makes electricity from natural gas with what is essentially a jet engine bolted to the ground. A compressor squeezes air, gas burns in it, and the hot blast spins a turbine that drives a generator. Most modern plants then use the exhaust to boil water for a second, steam turbine, turning about 60 percent of the fuel's energy into electricity.
cruise-missile: A pilotless jet plane that flies itself to its target. A jet engine keeps it flying low on short wings while an autopilot holds the course. The first ones simply counted the distance flown with a little propeller in the nose; modern ones steer by matching radar readings of the hills below to a stored map, and by GPS.
offshore-oil-platform: Pumps oil and gas from beneath the sea floor. A steel tower stands on legs pinned into the seabed, holding a deck above the waves with a drilling rig on top; a pipe is turned down through the water into the rock, and the oil and gas that come up are piped or shipped to shore.
defibrillator: Shocks a quivering heart back into a steady beat. When the heart's muscle fibres twitch out of step it pumps no blood; a capacitor charged to a few thousand volts dumps its charge through two pads on the chest in an instant, stopping every fibre at once so the heart's natural rhythm-setter can restart them together.
randomized-controlled-trial: A fair test of whether a treatment works. Patients are split into two groups purely by chance, for instance by sealed envelopes, and one group gets the treatment while the other does not. Chance spreads age, health and every hidden difference evenly, so any gap in how the groups fare is down to the treatment.
Austin Bradford Hill, Medical Research Council
disposable-diaper: A diaper you throw away instead of washing. A pad of fluffy, absorbent fibre wicks urine away from the baby's skin and holds it, and a waterproof plastic outer layer stops it leaking. Modern ones add grains of a powder that swells into a gel, holding many times its own weight of liquid.
cataract-lens-implant: Restores sight to people whose own lens has clouded over with age. The surgeon removes the cloudy lens and slips a small, clear plastic one into its place behind the iris, where it bends incoming light to a sharp focus on the retina. Ridley chose the plastic of fighter-plane canopies after seeing splinters of it lie harmlessly in pilots' eyes.
credit-card: Lets you buy now and pay later without carrying cash. The card names your account; the shop passes the charge to the card company, which pays the shop and sends you one bill a month. Later cards held the account number in a magnetic stripe, as tiny magnetised patches a reader senses, and now in a chip.
Frank McNamara and Ralph Schneider, Diners Club
hearing-aid: Makes sounds louder for people who are hard of hearing. A tiny microphone turns sound into a weak electric current, transistors amplify it, and a small earphone turns it back into louder sound in the ear. Transistors need far less battery power than the vacuum tubes they replaced, so aids shrank to fit in a pocket, then behind the ear.
tunnel-boring-machine: Digs tunnels for railways, roads and water through solid rock. A wheel as wide as the tunnel, studded with hard steel cutters, turns while hydraulic rams press it into the rock face; rolling disc cutters crack off chips, a conveyor carries them back, and the machine braces against the walls to push itself forward.
centre-pivot-irrigation: Waters a whole field with almost no labour. A long pipe carried on wheeled steel towers turns slowly round a well at the centre like the hand of a clock, spraying water from sprinklers along its length; each tower is driven forward by its own motor, so the arm sweeps out a giant green circle.
radiotherapy: Kills cancer cells with beams of radiation. In a linear accelerator, radio waves drive electrons along a tube to nearly the speed of light and smash them into a metal target to make powerful X-rays; the beam is shaped and swung round the patient from many angles, so it hits the tumour hardest and healthy tissue least.
hvdc-power-lines: Sends electricity hundreds of kilometres overland, or under the sea, losing less on the way than ordinary alternating current. At each end, banks of electronic switches turn AC into steady direct current and back. A steady current doesn't waste energy charging and discharging the cable's surroundings many times a second, and two wires do the work of three.
nuclear-submarine: A submarine that can stay underwater for months, not hours. In its reactor, splitting uranium heats water in a sealed loop; that water boils water in a second loop into steam, which spins a turbine to drive the propeller. Because nothing burns, it needs no air, and its time submerged is limited mainly by the crew's food.
transistor-radio: A radio small enough for a pocket that runs for weeks on one battery. Four transistors, tiny slivers of crystal that act as amplifiers, boost the faint signal picked up by a coil wound on a ferrite rod, doing the job of hot, power-hungry vacuum tubes, so the set needs no warm-up.
container-shipping: Moves the world's goods cheaply in steel boxes of standard sizes. Goods are packed once at the factory, and the same sealed box rides a truck, a ship and a train without being unpacked. Cranes grab each box by locking twist-fittings into its four top corners, so a ship is unloaded in hours instead of days.
disposable-syringe: Gives injections with a needle used once and thrown away, so it cannot carry disease from one patient to the next. A rubber-tipped plunger seals against the wall of a clear plastic barrel: pulling it back lowers the pressure inside, and the outside air pressure pushes medicine up through the hollow steel needle.
intercontinental-ballistic-missile: A rocket that can carry a nuclear warhead to another continent in about half an hour. Its liquid-fuel engines burn for only a few minutes, flinging the warhead above the atmosphere to coast down a long arc like a thrown stone. Gyroscopes sense every turn, so the guidance can cut the engines at exactly the right speed and direction.
wind-turbine: Makes electricity from the wind. Its long blades are shaped like aeroplane wings: air flowing past them creates lift that pulls each blade sideways, turning the rotor. A gearbox speeds up the slow spin to drive a generator at the top of the tower, and the whole head turns to face into the wind.
flexible-endoscope: Lets a doctor look inside the stomach without surgery. A bendable tube holds a bundle of thousands of glass fibres, each thinner than a hair and kept in the same order at both ends; light bounces along inside each fibre without escaping, so together they carry a picture round corners, while other fibres carry light in.
Basil Hirschowitz, Larry Curtiss, Wilbur Peters
spandex: A fibre that stretches to several times its length and springs back, used in sportswear, socks, waistbands and most stretch jeans. Its long molecules alternate soft, coiled, rubbery stretches with short stiff ones that stick to their neighbours; pulling uncoils the soft parts, and the stiff parts hold everything together so it snaps back.
liquefied-natural-gas-tanker: Carries natural gas across oceans where no pipeline can reach. Cooled to minus 162 °C, the gas turns to liquid and takes up only a six-hundredth of the space. It rides in heavily insulated tanks; the little that boils off carries heat away and keeps the rest cold, and the ship can burn it as fuel.
Constock and the British Gas Council
three-point-seat-belt: Holds you in your seat in a crash instead of letting you fly into the windscreen. One belt runs low across the hips and diagonally across the chest, anchored at three points, so the force lands on the strong pelvis and ribcage. A weighted catch in the reel locks the belt when the car brakes hard.
aluminium-drink-can: A light, unbreakable can for drinks that chills quickly and is easily recycled. A disc of aluminium is pressed into a shallow cup and then ironed up into a tall, thin-walled body in one piece; the domed bottom and the pressure of the drink inside keep the thin walls stiff, and a separate lid is folded onto the top.
turbofan-jet-engine: Pushes airliners along with less fuel and less noise than a plain jet. A big fan at the front, driven by a turbine at the back, blows most of its air around the outside of the engine's core; this broad, slower stream does most of the pushing, while the core burns fuel to keep the fan turning.
planetary-space-probes: A robot spacecraft sent to fly past or orbit another planet and report back. Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity, small thrusters keep it pointed the right way, and instruments measure what it passes. A dish antenna aimed at Earth sends the readings home as a faint radio signal that giant dishes pick up.
high-yield-dwarf-wheat-and-rice: Short, stiff grain plants that sharply raised harvests in Mexico and Asia in the 1960s. Fed with fertilizer, old tall varieties grew heavy heads and toppled over. Dwarfing genes from Japanese wheat and Taiwanese rice make the plant ignore part of a growth hormone's signal, so stalks stay short and upright and more of the plant goes into grain.
artificial-hip-joint-replacement: Replaces a hip joint worn out by arthritis, so people can walk again without pain. A polished steel ball on a stem is fixed into the hollow of the thigh bone with bone cement and turns inside a plastic cup cemented into the pelvis. The small ball and slippery plastic keep friction and wear low for decades.
carbon-fibre-composites: Makes parts stiffer and stronger than steel for their weight, for aircraft, racing bikes and tennis rackets. Threads of nearly pure carbon, each finer than a hair, are laid in the directions the load will pull and set in a hard, glue-like resin; the fibres carry the force and the resin holds them in shape.
William Watt, Leslie Phillips, William Johnson, Royal Aircraft Establishment
beta-blockers: Pills that calm the heart, used for angina, high blood pressure and irregular heartbeats. Adrenaline speeds and strengthens the heartbeat by fitting into receptor molecules on heart cells called beta receptors. A beta blocker fits into the same receptors without switching them on, so adrenaline can't get in and the heart beats slower and more gently.
high-speed-rail: Carries passengers between cities at over 200 kilometres an hour, often faster door to door than flying. Electric motors on every carriage draw power from an overhead wire through a sprung arm on the roof; the line is built with gentle curves, no level crossings and welded rails, so the train can run flat out.
drip-irrigation: Waters crops a drop at a time right at the roots, using far less water than flooding or sprinklers. Plastic tubes run along each row with small drippers set into them. Inside each dripper the water squeezes through a long, narrow zigzag channel whose friction soaks up the pressure, so it seeps out slowly and evenly all along the line.
night-vision-goggles: Lets soldiers, rescuers and wildlife watchers see by starlight. A lens focuses the faint light onto a coated plate where each particle of light knocks out an electron; a high voltage speeds the electrons up and multiplies them thousands of times, and they strike a phosphor screen that glows green with a bright copy of the scene.
dental-implant: Replaces a lost tooth with one that stays put. A small titanium screw is set into a hole drilled in the jawbone and left for some months; bone cells grow right up against the titanium and lock onto it, after which a false tooth is fixed to the top.
fax-machine: Sends a copy of a page across the world over an ordinary phone line. The sending machine scans the page line by line, a light-sensitive cell turning each spot's lightness or darkness into an electrical tone; the receiving machine listens to the tones and prints matching dots, line by line, to rebuild the page.
mammography: Finds breast cancer early, often before a lump can be felt. The breast is pressed flat between two plastic plates, and low-energy X-rays pass through it onto film or a detector. Tumours and tiny specks of calcium absorb more X-rays than the soft tissue around them, so they show up as white spots.
atm-cash-machine: Hands out banknotes at any hour. The machine reads the customer's card, from its magnetic stripe or chip, asks for a secret number and checks both with the bank's computer over a phone line; then rollers pull notes one by one from a stack, count them and push them out through a slot.
oral-rehydration-therapy: Saves people dying of diarrhoea with a drink of clean water, salt and sugar. Cholera makes the gut pour out water faster than a body can safely lose it. But the gut lining has carriers that pull salt and sugar in together, and water follows them by osmosis, so the drink is soaked up even while the diarrhoea goes on.
precision-guided-bombs: A bomb that steers itself onto its target, landing within a few metres instead of hundreds. A laser beam lights the target with invisible pulses; a sensor in the bomb's nose sees the reflected spot and moves small fins to keep it centred as the bomb glides down. Later kinds steer by satellite navigation instead.
Texas Instruments and the US Air Force
geographic-information-system: Lets planners, utilities, farmers and armies ask questions of maps by computer, such as which homes lie on flood-prone ground near a river. Each kind of information, from roads and soils to pipes and land use, is stored as its own layer pinned to the same map coordinates, so the computer can overlay them and pick out where conditions coincide.
quartz-watch: A watch accurate to a few seconds a month. A tiny quartz crystal rings thousands of times a second: squeezing quartz makes a voltage and a voltage makes it flex, so a battery-powered circuit can keep it ringing. A chip counts the vibrations and gives a little stepping motor one pulse a second to move the hands.
email: Sends a written message to someone's computer mailbox in seconds. The message is addressed with a person's name, an @ sign and the name of their computer, and is passed from machine to machine over the network until it reaches that one. There it waits in the person's mailbox file until they log in to read it.
video-game-console: Plays games on the family television. A TV draws its picture with a beam that sweeps across the screen line by line, and the console's circuits send a bright pulse at just the right moment in each sweep to put a square in a chosen spot. Turning a knob on a controller shifts that timing, so the square moves.
artemisinin-malaria-drug: Cures malaria fast, including strains that resist older drugs. It is extracted from sweet wormwood, a herb in old Chinese fever remedies; inside the red blood cells where the parasite lives, iron from digested blood snaps a fragile oxygen bridge in the molecule, releasing reactive fragments that wreck the parasite.
graphical-user-interface: Lets people use a computer by pointing at pictures instead of typing commands. Every dot on the screen is a bit in the computer's memory, so it can draw overlapping windows, icons and menus; a hand-held mouse moves an arrow across them, and clicking a picture carries out its command.
airbag: A cushion that bursts out of the steering wheel in a crash and catches the head before it hits. A sensor feels the sudden slowing and fires a pellet of chemicals that turns, in about a thirtieth of a second, into nitrogen gas filling a nylon bag; vents let the bag deflate as you land on it.
plastic-bottle: A light, shatterproof bottle that can hold fizzy drinks. A small test-tube shape of PET plastic is heated, stretched lengthwise by a rod and blown out against a mould by compressed air; the stretching lines up the plastic's long molecules in both directions, making the thin wall strong enough to hold the gas pressure.
local-area-network-ethernet: Wires the computers in an office or home together so they can share files, printers and the internet. Each machine sends data in short packets over a shared cable, listening first; if two start at the same moment, they hear the clash, both stop, and each waits a random instant before trying again. Today a switch usually gives each its own cable.
Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs, Xerox PARC
pulse-oximeter: Clips on a fingertip and shows how much oxygen the blood is carrying. Two tiny lights, one red and one infrared, shine through the finger to a light sensor on the other side. Oxygen-rich blood lets more red light through than oxygen-poor blood does, so comparing the two colours as each heartbeat swells the arteries gives the reading.
digital-camera: Takes photographs without film, so pictures can be seen at once and shared by computer. The lens focuses the scene onto an image-sensor chip, where light knocks electrons loose in each of millions of tiny squares; the camera measures the charge in each square and stores the numbers on a memory card.
pet-scanner: Shows which parts of the body are busiest, such as a tumour or a working patch of brain. The patient is injected with sugar carrying a radioactive tag that shoots out positrons, the antimatter twins of electrons; each meets an electron and both vanish into two gamma rays flying in opposite directions, which a ring of detectors catches.
Michael Phelps, Edward Hoffman, Michel Ter-Pogossian
monoclonal-antibodies: Antibody medicines and tests aimed at one exact target, now used against cancers, arthritis and many other diseases. A white blood cell that makes one chosen antibody is fused with a cancer cell, giving a hybrid that divides forever; all its descendants pour out identical Y-shaped antibodies whose tips lock onto one molecule and nothing else.
waterproof-breathable-fabric: Keeps rain out while letting sweat escape, so a jacket stays dry inside. A thin film of stretched non-stick plastic (PTFE) is bonded inside the cloth; it is full of billions of tiny pores, far too small for a raindrop to squeeze through but much bigger than single molecules of water vapour, which drift out.
Bob Gore, W. L. Gore & Associates
word-processor-software: Lets people type, correct and rearrange writing on a screen before anything is printed. The words sit in the computer's memory as a long string of character codes; inserting or deleting a letter just shifts the rest along, and the program re-flows the lines to fit the page, so a document can be revised endlessly and printed clean.
personal-computer: A whole computer for one person, on a desk at home or work. At its heart a single microprocessor chip fetches instructions from memory chips and carries them out one after another, from hundreds of thousands to billions of times a second. A keyboard and mouse put information in, a screen shows the results, and a disk keeps files.
public-key-encryption: Lets strangers exchange secrets over an open line; it guards every secure website and card payment. Each person hands out a lock anyone can close but keeps the only key; the lock is made by multiplying two huge prime numbers, which is easy, while recovering the primes from their product would take computers longer than the age of the universe.
Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, Leonard Adleman
anti-lock-brakes: Stops a car's wheels locking and skidding in hard braking, so the car can still be steered. A toothed ring and a magnetic sensor at each wheel report how fast it turns. If one wheel slows much faster than the car, a microchip has valves release and reapply its brake many times a second, keeping the tyre just short of skidding.
portable-music-player: Carries your music with you, played into lightweight headphones as you walk. The first ones played cassettes: a thin plastic tape coated with magnetised particles slides past a playback head, and the changing magnetism makes a tiny current that is amplified for the earphones. Later players store music as numbers in flash memory.
spreadsheet: Does a business's sums on screen and redoes them instantly when any figure changes. The screen is a grid of cells, each holding a number, a label or a formula that refers to other cells; change one number and the computer recalculates every cell that depends on it, so people can ask 'what if?'.
relational-database: Keeps the records of banks, airlines, hospitals and websites, letting thousands of people search and update them at once. Data sits in plain tables of rows and columns, linked by shared values such as a customer number; you state what you want in a short query language, and the software works out the fastest way to find and join the matching rows.
hepatitis-b-vaccine: Protects against a virus that causes liver failure and liver cancer; it was the first vaccine to prevent a cancer. It contains harmless copies of the virus's outer protein, which train the immune system to recognise the real thing; since 1986 that protein has been made by yeast cells given the virus gene, instead of purified from infected blood.
Baruch Blumberg, Irving Millman; Maurice Hilleman, Merck
home-blood-glucose-meter: Lets people with diabetes check their own blood sugar several times a day and adjust their insulin. A pricked finger puts a drop of blood on a strip whose pad holds an enzyme that reacts with sugar and darkens a dye; the meter shines a light on the pad and reads how much comes back, darker meaning more sugar.
ivermectin: Kills parasitic worms, mites and lice; yearly doses have nearly wiped out river blindness in parts of Africa. Made from a substance a soil bacterium produces, it jams open a gate found only in the nerve and muscle cells of worms and insects, so charged chlorine atoms flood in and the parasite is paralysed.
polar-fleece: A light, warm fabric that stays warm when wet and dries fast. Polyester fibres, often spun from melted-down plastic drinks bottles, are knitted into cloth whose surface is brushed up into a dense fuzz; the fuzz traps still air, which holds in body heat, and polyester soaks up almost no water.
ace-inhibitors: Pills that lower blood pressure and ease the strain on a failing heart. The body makes a hormone that squeezes blood vessels narrow, and an enzyme snips it into its active form. The drug, modelled on a peptide from a Brazilian snake's venom, plugs that enzyme, so the vessels relax and blood flows at lower pressure.
Miguel Ondetti and David Cushman, Squibb
compact-disc: Plays music stored as numbers on a shiny disc. A spiral track of microscopic pits is pressed into the plastic, and a laser shines up onto it while a light sensor reads the flicker of the reflection at each pit's edges. Extra check numbers mixed in let the player rebuild sound hidden by a scratch or a speck of dust.
computer-aided-design: Lets engineers and architects draw on a computer instead of a drawing board. Each line, arc and surface is stored as exact numbers, the coordinates of its ends and the curve between them, rather than as ink, so a drawing can be zoomed, measured, changed and copied without redrawing, and sent straight to machines that cut the parts.
computer-generated-imagery: Puts on screen things that were never in front of a camera, from film monsters to whole animated films. Every object is built as a mesh of tiny flat triangles; for each dot of the picture the computer works out how light from the lamps bounces off those surfaces into the camera, giving colour, shine and shadow, 24 pictures for every second of film.
solar-farm: Makes electricity from sunlight on the scale of a power station, now the cheapest new power in most of the world. Fields of silicon-cell panels turn light into direct current, each particle of light knocking an electron loose; inverters turn it into alternating current for the grid, and many panels sit on motorised mounts that tilt to follow the sun.
semiconductor-laser: A laser smaller than a grain of salt, cheap enough for every CD player and fibre-optic link. Current pushed into a thin layer of crystal, sandwiched between different crystals, makes electrons drop into holes and give off light; the sandwich traps both, and the polished ends act as mirrors, so the light bounces back and forth and builds into a narrow beam.
Robert N. Hall; Zhores Alferov; Izuo Hayashi and Morton Panish
recombinant-protein-drugs: Human hormones and proteins made in bulk by microbes, starting with insulin for diabetes, which until then came from pig and cow pancreases. The human gene is spliced into bacteria or yeast, which read it as one of their own and make the human protein; huge fermentation tanks grow them, and the protein is filtered out and purified.
pcr-dna-copying: Makes billions of copies of a chosen piece of DNA in a few hours, enough to test or read. The sample is heated so the two DNA strands come apart, then cooled so short starter pieces stick to each end of the target. An enzyme from hot-spring bacteria builds a new partner strand on each, doubling the target every cycle.
mobile-phone: A telephone you carry, so you can call from almost anywhere. The land is divided into small cells, each with its own radio mast; the phone talks to the nearest one and is handed on to the next as you move. Cells far enough apart reuse the same frequencies, so millions of people can call at once.
stealth-aircraft: A warplane that radar can barely see. Its skin is made of flat, angled panels that bounce radar waves off in a few directions away from the transmitter, like a tilted mirror, instead of back to it; special coatings soak up much of the rest as heat, so even a large jet returns only a faint echo.
insecticide-treated-bed-nets: Protects sleepers from the night-biting mosquitoes that spread malaria. A net over the bed keeps mosquitoes off, and its fibres are soaked or coated with insecticide, so mosquitoes that land on the mesh trying to get in are killed or driven away, even where the net is torn; when most homes use them, malaria falls for the whole village.
internet: Links the world's computer networks into one. Every message is chopped into small packets, each labelled with where it is going; routers along the way pass each packet on toward its destination by whatever path is free, and the receiving computer puts them back in order and asks again for any that went missing.
anti-rejection-drugs: Stops the body rejecting a transplanted kidney, liver or heart, and made those operations routine. It comes from a fungus found in a Norwegian soil sample. Inside the immune system's T cells it shuts down a signalling enzyme, so the cells that would attack the foreign organ never switch on; unlike older drugs it spares the bone marrow.
digital-synthesizer-and-midi: Lets one keyboard or computer play and record a whole band of electronic instruments. A digital synthesizer builds sounds by arithmetic: in the common FM method, one fast wave wobbles the pitch of another, making rich bell- and brass-like tones. A standard cable sends notes as short numbered messages, which key and how hard, so any instrument can play any other.
John Chowning, Yamaha; Dave Smith and Ikutaro Kakehashi
neodymium-magnet: The strongest permanent magnet, small enough for earbuds and strong enough for electric-car motors and wind turbines. An alloy of neodymium, iron and boron is ground to powder, lined up in a magnetic field, pressed and baked solid, then magnetised; its crystals hold their magnetism so stubbornly that a disc the size of a coin can lift several kilograms of steel.
Masato Sagawa, Sumitomo Special Metals; John Croat, General Motors
active-matrix-lcd: The flat colour screen of laptops, televisions and phones. Each dot of the picture is a tiny window of liquid crystal between polarising filters, which twists light more or less to let it through. Printed on the glass behind each dot is its own transistor switch, which holds the voltage steady between refreshes, so a big screen stays sharp, fast and bright.
desktop-publishing: Lets one person with a computer lay out a newsletter, magazine or book that prints looking professionally typeset. Text and pictures are arranged on an on-screen page that matches the printed one; the page goes to a laser printer as a description of shapes, so each letter is drawn from its outline at the printer's full sharpness.
dna-fingerprinting: Identifies a person, or their parents, from a speck of blood, hair or saliva. Everyone's DNA has short stretches repeated over and over, the number of repeats differing between people. The DNA is cut up and pulled through jelly by an electric current, which sorts the pieces by length into a pattern of bands unique to each person.
coronary-stent: Keeps a clogged heart artery open after it has been widened, without open-heart surgery. A tiny tube of metal mesh, crimped onto a deflated balloon, is threaded up through an artery from the wrist or groin; at the narrowing the balloon inflates, pressing the mesh into the wall, then deflates and is pulled out, leaving the mesh as permanent scaffolding.
3d-printing: Builds a solid object straight from a computer design, one thin layer at a time. In the first machines an ultraviolet laser traces the shape of one slice on the surface of a vat of liquid plastic, which hardens where the light falls. The platform then sinks a fraction of a millimetre and the next slice is drawn on top.
statins: Pills that lower blood cholesterol and cut the risk of heart attacks and strokes. The liver makes much of the body's cholesterol through a chain of chemical steps. A statin jams the enzyme that runs one early step, so the liver makes less and pulls more cholesterol out of the blood to make up the shortfall.
flash-memory: Keeps photos, music and files when the power is off, in phones, cameras and memory sticks. Each bit is a little charge of electrons trapped on an island of conductor sealed in very thin insulation above a transistor. A high voltage pushes electrons through the insulation by quantum tunnelling, and the trapped charge decides whether the transistor switches on.
keyhole-surgery: Operations through cuts a centimetre long instead of opening the body, so patients go home in days rather than weeks. The belly is puffed up with carbon dioxide to make room; a thin telescope lit through glass fibres sends a camera picture to a screen, while the surgeon works with long, slender instruments through other small holes.
antidepressants-ssris: Eases depression and anxiety with fewer side effects than older pills. Nerve cells pass signals by releasing a messenger chemical, serotonin, into the narrow gap between them and then soaking it back up; the drug blocks that soaking-up pump, so serotonin lingers in the gap and keeps passing its signal.
David Wong, Bryan Molloy, Ray Fuller, Eli Lilly
rolling-suitcase: Lets travellers pull their luggage instead of carrying it. Two small wheels are set into the bottom corners of an upright case, and a handle slides up out of the top on telescoping tubes; tipping the case back onto its wheels puts most of its weight over the axle, so the hand only steadies it and pulls.
conjugate-vaccines: Protects babies from meningitis and pneumonia caused by bacteria with a sugary coat. Young children's immune systems ignore sugars, so a vaccine of the coat alone fails them; chemically bolting the sugar onto a harmless protein brings the immune system's helper cells in, and the child makes lasting antibodies against the coat.
John Robbins and Rachel Schneerson, US National Institutes of Health
rapid-test-strip: Gives a yes-or-no medical answer in minutes at home, as in pregnancy and Covid tests. A drop of urine or swab fluid soaks along a paper strip, picking up antibodies stuck to tiny coloured particles; if the substance being tested for is there, it links those particles to a line of other antibodies fixed across the strip, and a coloured line appears.
Unipath, Unilever (Keith May, Mick Prior, Ian Richards)
medical-abortion-pill: Ends an early pregnancy with pills instead of surgery. A pregnancy needs the hormone progesterone to keep the lining of the womb in place; mifepristone fits into the cells' progesterone receptors without switching them on, so the lining breaks down. A second drug, misoprostol, taken a day or two later makes the womb contract and empty.
proton-pump-inhibitors: Pills that heal stomach ulcers and stop heartburn by cutting stomach acid. Cells in the stomach lining push acid out with tiny molecular pumps. The drug passes the stomach inside an acid-proof coating and is absorbed into the blood; in the acid around those cells it turns into a form that locks onto the pumps and jams them for a day.
fly-by-wire-airliner: An airliner whose controls are worked by computers instead of cables and pulleys. The pilot's small side-stick sends electrical signals to computers, which also read gyroscopes and accelerometers; they then drive hydraulic rams that move the wing and tail surfaces, and refuse any command that would stall the plane or overstress it.
laser-eye-surgery: Corrects short sight so people can do without glasses. An ultraviolet laser fires short pulses at the clear front of the eye; each pulse breaks the chemical bonds in a layer of tissue far thinner than a hair, vaporising it without heating what's around it. Flattening the cornea's curve this way moves the eye's focus back onto the retina.
direct-to-home-satellite-tv: Brings hundreds of TV channels to any home with a clear view of the sky. A satellite 36,000 km above the equator circles once a day, so it hangs over one spot and beams down microwaves; a small dish focuses them onto a receiver head, which amplifies the faint signal and lowers its frequency so it can run down a cable to the TV.
lithium-ion-battery: The light, rechargeable battery in phones, laptops and electric cars. Charging drives lithium ions out of a layered metal-oxide crystal, through a liquid, and slips them between the layers of graphite in the other electrode; using the battery lets them drift back while electrons flow the long way round, through the device.
Akira Yoshino, John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham; Sony
world-wide-web: Turns the internet into a library anyone can browse. Pages are stored on computers called servers, each page with its own address; a browser program asks for a page, gets back text marked up with formatting and links, and clicking a link fetches another page from wherever in the world it lives.
digital-cellular-network-2g: Made mobile phones cheap enough for billions of people, with clearer calls and text messages. The phone turns speech into compressed numbers and sends them in short bursts; each radio channel is shared by eight calls taking turns, each getting one time slot in eight. A small chip card in the phone, the SIM, proves who is paying.
unicode-text-encoding: Lets computers store and show text in every writing system, from English and Arabic to Chinese and emoji, without garbling it. Each character in the world's scripts gets its own number, over 150,000 so far, and every computer agrees on them; a compact scheme stores common letters in one byte and rarer ones in up to four.
Joe Becker, Lee Collins and Mark Davis
open-source-operating-system: Free software that runs most of the world's servers, supercomputers and phones, written by thousands of volunteers and companies. Its source code, the human-readable instructions, is published for anyone to read, change and share; changes are sent in over the Internet, reviewed, and merged by maintainers into the next version, which anyone can download.
compressed-media: Squeezes music and pictures to a tenth of their size or less, so they fit on small devices and travel quickly over the internet. Sound is split into narrow bands of pitch, and quiet sounds that the ear can't hear next to louder ones are thrown away. Photos are trimmed the same way, dropping fine detail the eye won't miss.
mems-motion-sensors: The accelerometer shrunk onto a silicon chip, cheap enough to fire airbags and turn phone screens. Etching carves a tiny weight hung on silicon springs, with comb-like fingers interleaved with fixed ones; when the chip speeds up or tilts, the weight lags, the gaps between the fingers change, and the chip senses the change in stored electric charge.
electric-bicycle-2000s: A bicycle with a battery-powered motor that adds to the rider's push, making hills and long commutes easy for hundreds of millions of people. A sensor in the pedal crank measures how hard the rider presses and the motor adds a matching push; many, especially in China, are simply worked by a twist grip like a scooter's.
text-messaging-sms: Sends a short typed message from one mobile phone to another, delivered even if the other phone is switched off. The message, up to 160 characters, rides on the radio channel the network already uses to set up calls; a message centre holds it and keeps trying until the phone reappears, then passes it on.
genetically-modified-crops: Crops given a useful gene borrowed from another living thing. The gene is slipped into plant cells by a bacterium that naturally inserts DNA into plants, or shot in on tiny gold beads, and whole plants are grown from the changed cells. A common example makes a bacterial protein that poisons caterpillars, so the plant protects itself.
online-shopping: Lets people buy almost anything from home and have it delivered. A shop's website lists its goods; the customer's card number is scrambled by encryption on its way to the shop's computer, which checks it with the bank, and a warehouse then picks, packs and posts the order.
qr-code: Stores a web address, ticket or payment in a square of black and white blocks that any phone camera can read. Three large corner squares tell the reader where the code is and which way up it lies, so it reads at any angle; extra error-correcting blocks let it be read even with nearly a third of it smudged or torn.
online-banking: Lets people check balances, pay bills and move money from home at any hour. The bank's website, reached over a secure web connection, asks for a password, then reads the bank's own account records for that customer, and turns each payment typed in into an instruction that the bank's computers carry out.
military-drones: An aircraft with no one aboard that watches or strikes from far away, flown by a crew on the ground, perhaps on another continent. A camera ball under the nose sends live video up to a satellite and down to the crew, whose commands return the same way; long, thin wings let it circle for a day.
electronic-stability-control: Stops a car skidding out of a bend. Sensors compare where the driver is steering with how fast the car is really turning; if it starts to spin or plough straight on, a computer brakes one wheel, the outer front to stop a spin or the inner rear to tighten the turn, pulling the car back onto line.
home-broadband-dsl-and-cable-modem: Gives homes an always-on internet connection tens of times faster than dialling up, over wires already there. A cable-TV line carries data in a few spare TV channels. A phone line, built for voice, is split into hundreds of narrow frequency bands above the pitch of speech, each carrying as much data as its noise allows, while calls go on underneath.
secure-web-connection-ssl-tls: Keeps passwords and card numbers secret on their way between your browser and a website, and proves the site is genuine. The site presents a certificate vouched for by a trusted authority; the browser uses public-key encryption to agree a fresh secret key with the site, then scrambles everything sent both ways with that key.
antiretroviral-hiv-therapy: Turns HIV infection from a death sentence into a condition people live with. The virus copies its genes into the cell's DNA with an enzyme called reverse transcriptase, then needs a second enzyme, protease, to finish new viruses; the drugs jam these enzymes. Taking three at once means the virus would need several lucky mutations together to escape.
white-led-lighting: Lights homes and streets on a fraction of a bulb's electricity and lasts for decades. A tiny chip of gallium nitride glows blue when current flows through it; a coating of yellow phosphor over the chip turns some of that blue light into yellow, and the blue and yellow together look white.
contactless-card: Pays a fare or a bill with a tap, with no battery in the card. A coil of wire loops around the card's edge; the reader's coil makes a rapidly changing magnetic field that induces a current in it, powering the chip, which answers by switching its coil's load on and off, a flicker the reader detects.
universal-serial-port-usb: One plug that connects keyboards, mice, drives and chargers to any computer. When a device is plugged in, the computer asks what it is; the device answers with a description of itself, and the computer loads the right software, no restart needed. Data then travels one bit after another down a pair of twisted wires, while two more wires carry power.
electronic-voting-machine: Counts a whole country's votes within hours, with no paper ballots to lose or misread. The voter presses numbered keys for a candidate and sees their name and photo on a small screen before confirming; each vote is stored in sealed memory, and when the polls close the machine prints a tally and its encrypted results are sent on for adding up.
mars-rovers: A robot car that drives across Mars studying rocks. Solar panels power it, and its six wheels ride on pivoting arms that let it climb over stones while keeping every wheel on the ground. Radio signals take minutes to reach Earth, so between commands it steers itself around obstacles using its own cameras.
streaming-video: Plays video over the internet as it arrives, instead of waiting for the whole file to download. The video is heavily compressed and sent as a stream of small packets; the player keeps a few seconds in hand and shows them in order while more arrive. Modern players drop to lower quality on the fly when the connection slows.
wi-fi: Connects laptops, phones and printers to the internet without cables, across a home or office. A router and each device trade short radio bursts at a few billion waves a second. Newer versions split the data across dozens of neighbouring frequencies sent at once, which the receiving chip separates by Fourier analysis, so echoes off walls do not scramble it.
hybrid-car: Burns much less fuel in stop-start town driving. A petrol engine and an electric motor share the job of turning the wheels; when the car brakes, the motor runs as a generator and charges a battery instead of wasting the energy as heat, and that stored power helps the car pull away again.
social-media: Lets people keep up with friends and share news, photos and opinions with anyone. Each person makes a profile and links to friends; a central website stores everyone's posts and, every time someone looks, a program assembles a fresh feed from the people they follow, picking and ordering what to show.
ion-thruster: Pushes a spacecraft for months on end using a tenth of a rocket's fuel. Powered by solar panels, it strips electrons off xenon atoms, and charged metal grids at the back fling the ions out at about 30 kilometres a second. The push is as gentle as a sheet of paper resting on your hand, but never lets up.
search-engine: Finds the few pages that answer a question among billions on the web. Programs crawl the web, copying every page and indexing every word; pages matching the question are then ranked, each scoring higher the more links point to it, especially links from pages that themselves rank high.
fracking: Gets gas and oil out of dense shale rock that would otherwise hold on to it. A well is drilled down and then sideways along the rock layer; water with sand is pumped in at enormous pressure to split the rock into fine cracks, and the sand grains wedge the cracks open so the gas can seep out.
cmos-camera-chip: The camera inside every phone, laptop and car. A grid of millions of light-sensitive spots on a silicon chip turns light into electric charge; unlike the older CCD chip, each spot has its own tiny amplifier, and the same cheap chip carries the circuits that read out and digitise the picture, so it needs little power.
Eric Fossum, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
continuous-glucose-monitor-insulin-pump: Tracks blood sugar day and night for people with diabetes, without finger-prick tests. A hair-thin wire under the skin is coated with an enzyme that reacts with sugar in the body's fluid, making a tiny electric current: more sugar, more current. A small transmitter turns that into a reading every few minutes and can pass it to an insulin pump.
short-range-wireless-link: Links earbuds, keyboards, watches and speakers to a phone or computer across a room. Each device sends weak radio signals at 2.4 billion waves a second and hops between 79 channels 1,600 times a second, in a pattern both ends know, so it dodges interference from other gadgets nearby.
graphics-processor-gpu: Draws the moving pictures of video games, and now does the heavy arithmetic of artificial intelligence. A screen has millions of dots, and working out each one's colour is the same small sum done over and over, so the chip packs hundreds or thousands of simple arithmetic units side by side, each taking a share and all working at once.
emoji: Little pictures typed into messages, so a smile, a heart or a thumbs-up travels with the words. Each emoji is stored as a number code, just like a letter, so any phone can send it; the receiving phone looks the code up in its own font and draws its own picture, which is why the same emoji looks slightly different on different phones.
robotic-surgery: Lets a surgeon operate through a few small cuts using robot arms. Thin instruments and a 3D camera on long rods go in through the cuts, while the surgeon sits at a console watching the magnified view and working hand controls. Computers scale down every movement and filter out tremor, and tiny wrists at the instrument tips bend like a hand.
ready-to-use-therapeutic-food: Lets starving children recover at home instead of in a hospital ward. It is a thick paste of peanuts, milk powder, sugar, oil, vitamins and minerals in a sealed foil packet; because it holds almost no water, germs cannot grow in it, so it keeps for two years without a fridge and a child can eat it straight from the packet.
kinase-inhibitor-cancer-drugs: Pills that hold some cancers in check for years, first of all a leukaemia that used to be fatal. Some cancers are driven by one faulty enzyme, a kinase stuck 'on', that keeps telling cells to divide. The drug is a small molecule shaped to fit the pocket where that kinase takes in its fuel, plugging it so the signal stops.
smart-electricity-meter: Measures a home's electricity and reports it to the power company by itself, so no one has to read the dial and prices can change by the hour. A chip samples the voltage and current thousands of times a second and multiplies them to get the power used; a modem sends the totals back over the power wires or by radio.
mobile-broadband-3g-data: Brings the internet to a phone, fast enough for web pages, maps and video calls. Every phone transmits across the same wide band of radio at once, each signal mixed with its own fast code; the mast picks out each phone by matching that code, and data moves in packets only when there is something to send.
online-encyclopedia-wiki: A free encyclopedia that anyone with a web browser can read and edit, with millions of articles in hundreds of languages. Every page has an edit button; each change is saved as a new version, so nothing is lost and a bad edit can be undone in one click, while volunteers watch the stream of recent changes and argue out disputes on discussion pages.
video-calling: Lets people talk face to face across the world, seeing each other as they speak. A small camera captures about thirty pictures a second; software squeezes them by sending mostly what changed since the last picture, breaks them into packets and sends them over the internet, where the other computer rebuilds and shows them alongside the sound.
electronic-cigarette: Delivers nicotine in a mist instead of smoke, with nothing burning. A battery heats a small wire coil wound around a wick soaked in liquid: propylene glycol, glycerine, flavouring and nicotine. The liquid flash-boils off the hot wick, and the vapour cools in the air being sucked through into tiny droplets that the user breathes in.
podcasting: Free audio shows, made by anyone, that arrive on your phone or music player by themselves. The maker records an episode, saves it as a compressed sound file and adds it to a web feed, a running list on their website; the listener's app checks the feed every few hours and downloads anything new, ready to play offline.
rotavirus-vaccine: Drops swallowed by babies that protect them from rotavirus, the commonest cause of deadly diarrhoea in young children. The drops hold live but weakened virus, grown in the lab until it barely makes anyone ill; it multiplies a little in the baby's gut and trains the immune system to fight off the real thing.
glp-1-drugs: Medicines that help people with diabetes control their blood sugar, and help many lose weight. They copy a gut hormone released after meals that tells the pancreas to release insulin, slows the stomach, and tells the brain you are full. The body's own hormone is broken down in minutes; the drugs are altered to last a day or a week.
John Eng; Amylin and Eli Lilly
online-maps-and-navigation: Shows any street on Earth, finds the way there and talks you through each turn. The world's maps and satellite photos are cut into square tiles at many zoom levels, so a phone fetches only the few it needs; satellite positioning places you on them, and distant computers plan the route using speed reports from millions of other phones to avoid traffic jams.
distributed-version-control: Lets thousands of programmers work on the same code at once without overwriting each other. Every programmer keeps a full copy of the project and its whole history; each saved change is labelled with a fingerprint calculated from its contents, so copies can be compared and swapped over the Internet, and the software merges different people's edits line by line.
cloud-data-centres: Lets people and companies rent computing power and storage over the internet instead of owning machines. Warehouse-sized buildings hold tens of thousands of computers in racks; software spreads each job and copies each file across many of them, so any one can fail unnoticed. Most of the electricity ends up as heat, which fans and chilled water carry away.
machine-translation: Translates text, signs and speech between dozens of languages in an instant, for free. The computer learns from millions of documents that exist in two languages, such as United Nations records, finding which words and phrases usually match which; given new text, it assembles the most likely translation. Since 2016 neural networks have done this a whole sentence at a time.
hpv-vaccine: Prevents infection with the viruses behind most cervical cancers and several others. Yeast given one virus gene makes the virus's outer-shell protein, which assembles itself into empty shells that look just like the real virus but carry no genes. The immune system learns to recognise the shells and later blocks the real virus.
smartphone: A pocket computer that is also a telephone, camera, map and music player. A glass touchscreen senses fingers by the electric charge they draw, and inside are radios for calls, data and satellite positioning, a camera chip and a lithium-ion battery. A microscopic weight on springs inside a chip senses tilt, so the screen turns to match the phone.
mobile-money: Lets people without a bank account send and keep money using a basic mobile phone. Cash handed to a local shop agent becomes credit held by the phone company; the owner sends it to anyone with a short text message and a PIN, and the receiver turns it back into cash at another agent.
oled-display-2000s: The screen in most smartphones and many TVs, thin enough to bend, where each dot makes its own light. Every pixel is a sandwich of thin films of carbon-based molecules between two electrodes; current pushed through makes them glow red, green or blue, and a tiny transistor behind each one sets its brightness. With no backlight, black pixels are simply off.
Ching Tang and Steven Van Slyke, Kodak
direct-oral-anticoagulants: Pills that prevent dangerous blood clots and strokes without the blood tests and diet rules of the older warfarin. Clotting is a chain of enzymes, each switching on the next until threads of fibrin knit a clot. These drugs fit into one enzyme near the end of the chain, thrombin or factor Xa, and block it directly, so a fixed dose works predictably.
off-grid-solar-lighting: Gives homes without electricity clean, bright light in place of smoky kerosene lamps. A small solar panel charges a lithium-ion battery during the day; at night the battery powers a white LED, which turns electricity into light so efficiently that a few hours of sunshine runs the lamp all evening, and often charges a phone too.
Sam Goldman and Ned Tozun, d.light
grid-battery-storage: Steadies the electricity grid and stores cheap solar and wind power for later. Thousands of lithium-ion cells fill rows of container-sized cabinets, and inverters turn their direct current into the grid's alternating current. When a power station trips and the grid's frequency starts to sag, they push out power within a fraction of a second, far faster than any spinning generator.
quadcopter-drone: A small flying camera that anyone can steer. Four propellers on electric motors lift it, two spinning clockwise and two anticlockwise so the craft doesn't twirl; a computer reads tiny gyroscopes hundreds of times a second and speeds up or slows each motor to keep it level, tilt it and steer.
cyberweapons: Software built to wreck a country's machinery, not just steal its secrets. The first known one, found in 2010, slipped into Iran's uranium plant on memory sticks through software flaws nobody knew of, hunted for the controllers of its centrifuges and made them spin too fast and then too slow, breaking them, while showing the operators normal readings.
biometric-digital-id: Gives each person a number they can prove is theirs with a fingertip or an eye, even with no papers.
