At enrolment ten fingerprints, both irises and the face are recorded and checked against everyone on file, so nobody gets two numbers; later a scanner at a bank or shop sends a fingerprint to the central computers, which answer yes or no.
Unique Identification Authority of India, Nandan Nilekani
ride-hailing-apps: Summons a car to wherever you are standing with a tap on a phone. The phone sends its satellite-positioning fix to the company's computers, which track every nearby driver on a live map, pick the closest free one, set the fare from distance and demand, and charge your card when the ride ends. Most drivers are ordinary people in their own cars.
voice-assistants: Answers spoken questions and carries out spoken requests. A microphone records the voice, and software trained on huge amounts of recorded speech turns the sounds into words. Other programs work out what was meant, find an answer or take an action, and a speech synthesiser reads the reply aloud.
rocket-interceptor-system: Shoots down rockets fired at towns, while ignoring those headed for empty ground. A radar tracks each rocket moments after launch and a computer predicts where it will land; only if that is a populated area does it fire an interceptor missile, steered by radio updates and then its own radar to explode beside the rocket in mid-air.
cancer-immunotherapy: Lets the body's own immune system destroy cancer, sometimes for good, even after it has spread. Killer white blood cells carry brakes, switch proteins that stop them attacking the body's own tissue, and many tumours press those brakes. The drugs are antibodies that cover the brake switches, so the killer cells go back to attacking the tumour.
prenatal-dna-blood-test: Checks an unborn baby for Down syndrome and some other conditions from a sample of the mother's blood, with no needle into the womb. Tiny fragments of the baby's DNA, shed by the placenta, float in her blood; the test reads millions of fragments and counts which chromosome each came from, so an extra copy of one shows up as a small surplus.
crispr-gene-editing: Lets scientists change a chosen spot in the DNA of a living cell, to breed crops or treat inherited disease. A protein called Cas9 carries a short strand of RNA that matches the target; it slides along the DNA until the letters pair up, then cuts both strands. As the cell repairs the cut, the gene is disabled or rewritten.
deep-learning: Lets computers recognise faces, speech and objects in photos by learning from examples rather than rules. Each example passes through many stacked layers of simple number-crunching units; whenever the answer comes out wrong, every connection is nudged slightly in the direction that would have shrunk the error, millions of times over.
Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Geoffrey Hinton
sglt2-inhibitors: Pills for diabetes that also protect the heart and kidneys. The kidneys filter sugar out of the blood and then pull nearly all of it back in through tiny pumps lining their tubes. The drug blocks the main pump, so around 70 grams of surplus sugar a day leaves in the urine instead of staying in the blood.
software-containers: Packs a program with everything it needs, so it runs the same on a laptop as on a thousand servers. The operating system walls each container off, giving it its own view of files and network and a fixed share of memory and processor, while all of them share one system underneath, so they start in a second and pack many to a machine.
hepatitis-c-cure: Cures a liver virus carried by tens of millions with two or three months of daily pills. The virus copies its genes with its own enzyme; the drug mimics one of the building blocks that enzyme uses, so the enzyme builds it into the new copy and copying stops dead. Paired with a second drug, it clears the virus in over 95% of people.
reusable-rocket-booster: Brings a rocket's first stage back to land after launch, so it can fly again and spaceflight costs less. The booster flips around and relights its engines to slow down, steering through the air with lattice fins near its top. It fires once more just before touchdown, unfolds four legs and settles upright on a pad or a floating barge.
smartwatch-and-fitness-tracker: A wristwatch that counts steps, tracks sleep, measures the heartbeat and shows messages from the phone. A tiny accelerometer chip feels every step and movement; on the back, green lights shine into the wrist and a light sensor picks up the faint pulsing as blood, which soaks up green light, surges through the vessels with each heartbeat.
stroke-clot-retrieval: Pulls the blood clot out of a blocked brain artery during a stroke, often sparing the patient lasting disability. Guided by X-ray, a doctor threads a thin tube from the groin up into the brain and pushes a folded wire-mesh tube through the clot; the mesh springs open, the clot gets caught in it, and both are drawn back out.
short-video-feed-apps: An endless stream of short phone videos, picked for each viewer by a learning program. Every swipe, replay and pause is recorded; the program compares it with the behaviour of millions of others to predict which clip will hold this viewer longest, shows that one next, and keeps retraining itself on what people actually watch.
end-to-end-encrypted-messaging: Lets people text and call so that nobody in between, not even the company running the service, can read the messages. Each phone keeps its own secret keys and uses public-key encryption to agree a shared key with the other phone; the key changes with every message, so a key stolen today cannot unlock older messages.
facial-recognition: Recognises a person from their face, to unlock a phone, check a passport or pick someone out of a crowd. A neural network trained on millions of photos turns each face into a list of numbers, a point in a space where pictures of the same person land close together; the system checks how close a new face is to stored ones.
viral-vector-vaccines: Vaccines that use a harmless virus to deliver one gene from a dangerous one. The carrier virus, stripped so it cannot cause disease, gets into cells near the injection and makes them build the target virus's surface protein, which the immune system learns to attack. An Ebola vaccine and some Covid-19 vaccines, given billions of times, work this way.
Public Health Agency of Canada; Merck
self-driving-cars: A car that drives itself with nobody at the wheel. A spinning laser rangefinder on the roof measures the distance to everything around it millions of times a second, building a 3D picture, while cameras and radar add more. Deep-learning software picks out cars, people and lanes in that picture and plans a path, steering and braking on its own.
mrna-vaccines: Teaches the immune system to recognise a virus without meeting it. The injection carries genetic instructions for one virus protein, wrapped in tiny bubbles of fat; muscle cells read the instructions and make the protein, which the immune system learns to attack. The instructions fall apart within days, and the vaccine can be redesigned for a new virus in weeks.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman; BioNTech, Moderna
satellite-internet-constellations: Brings fast internet to remote places with no cables. Thousands of small satellites circle only about 550 kilometres up, so signals make the trip quickly; a flat dish on the roof steers its beam electronically to whichever satellite is passing overhead, handing over to the next every few minutes, and the satellites relay the data to ground stations.
large-language-models: Answers questions, writes and translates in everyday language. A huge neural network is trained on a vast library of text to predict the next word, adjusting billions of internal settings until it gets good at it; to reply, it predicts one word after another, each time feeding everything so far back in.
ai-image-generation: Makes a picture of whatever you describe in words. A neural network is trained by taking millions of captioned images, adding random speckle, and learning to remove it; to make a new picture it starts from pure speckle and cleans it away in dozens of small steps, each guided by the words, until an image appears.
OpenAI; LMU Munich and Stability AI
fpv-attack-drone: A cheap racing drone turned into a guided bomb. The pilot wears video goggles showing the live view from a small camera in the drone's nose, as if sitting aboard, and steers it by radio straight into a tank, trench or vehicle, where an explosive charge strapped under it goes off. Each costs a few hundred dollars.
centrifugal-pump: Moves water by flinging it. A spinning wheel of curved vanes throws water outward into a snail-shaped casing, which slows it into pressure, while more water is drawn into the centre. Appold's pump at the 1851 Great Exhibition made it practical; it now drains, waters and circulates almost everything.
jet-engine: Pushes an aircraft by throwing hot gas backward. A compressor at the front squeezes air, fuel burns in it, and the hot gas spins a turbine that drives the compressor before rushing out of the nozzle. Whittle ran the first one on a test bench in 1937; von Ohain's flew first, in 1939.
phosphor: A powder that glows when struck. Crystals such as zinc sulphide soak up electrons, ultraviolet or blue light and give the energy back as visible light of their own colour. Sidot made the first lasting one in 1866; phosphors lit every television tube and now turn blue LEDs white.
accelerometer: Senses speeding up, slowing down and tilting. A small mass on a spring lags behind when its case moves, and the stretch of the spring, read electrically, measures the acceleration. Early ones guided missiles; shrunk onto chips in the 1990s, they fire airbags and turn phone screens.
boiling-points: Every liquid boils at its own temperature, and that temperature rises when the pressure on it rises and falls when it drops. Fahrenheit found in 1724 that water's boiling point shifts with the weather's air pressure. It's why stills can separate liquids, pressure cookers cook faster and hot water underground flashes into steam.
plants-need-water: A growing plant draws a great deal of water up from its roots and breathes most of it out through its leaves; without a steady supply it wilts and stops growing. Hales weighed potted plants in 1727 and measured how much water they pass. Irrigation of every kind exists to meet that need.
